question: One of Spain’s Deputy Prime Ministers has made public statements singling out a judge in a television interview. Teresa Ribera, the Third Vice-President of the Spanish Government, said that a National High Court judge was deeply involved in politics after that judge had stated that the Supreme Court should investigate Carles Puigdemont, a fugitive from justice, for terrorist offences.

Spain’s Council for the Judiciary responded to this serious declaration and accusation on the part of the Spanish Government by stating that the claims were at odds with the principle of institutional loyalty and the general duty of respecting judicial independence. These are inherent to the rule of law of a Member State of the European Union, and the separation of powers is an essential element of that.

The Council for the Judiciary maintained that these statements by the government should be roundly condemned, especially if they interfere with an ongoing investigation into the facts of the matter. Three of the four judges’ associations have condemned Ribera’s attack on Judge García Castellón and called for the government to show respect. 1.
What is the Commission’s view of the targeting of judges, especially when it comes from a member of the government?
Will it urge the Spanish Government to respect the separation of powers and ensure institutional loyalty?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.5.2024) The Commission is aware of the issue raised by the Honourable Member. Already in 2022 and 2023 Country Chapters on the rule of law situation in Spain1, the Commission underlined that stakeholders had raised concerns of public statements by politicians, including members of Parliament and the Government, criticising the judiciary.

In this context, the Commission recalled that, ‘according to European standards, while courts are not immune to criticism and scrutiny, the judiciary must enjoy public confidence to be successful in view of its special role in society.

This is particularly important in relation to statements by members of the legislative and the executive branches, as all powers of the State must foster and protect the trust of the general public in constitutional institutions including the judiciary’2.

The Commission remains committed to taking any necessary measures to ensure compliance with EU law and upholding the rule of law in all Member States, and will continue to work with the Spanish authorities to promote the rule of law within the framework of the rule of law cycle.
